nameStory: Kentucky yellowwood gets its name from its bright yellow heartwood, which was once prized for making yellow dye. When you cut into the wood, it reveals a beautiful golden-yellow color that contrasts sharply with the pale sapwood. The 'Kentucky' part of the name comes from the tree being first scientifically described from specimens found in Kentucky, though it actually grows throughout much of the southeastern United States.
description: Kentucky yellowwood is a medium-sized deciduous tree that reaches 30-50 feet tall with a broad, rounded crown. It's a member of the legume family, producing drooping clusters of fragrant white flowers that look almost like wisteria blooms. The smooth, gray bark and compound leaves with oval leaflets give it an elegant appearance. This native southeastern tree is occasionally planted as an ornamental in New England for its spectacular spring flower display.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Drooping clusters of fragrant white flowers, 8-14 inches long, that hang like grape bunches from the branches in late spring. Each individual flower is pea-like with five petals and smells sweetly fragrant.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with 7-11 smooth-edged, oval leaflets arranged alternately on the stem. The leaflets feel smooth and papery, turning bright yellow in fall before dropping.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Smooth, thin gray bark that feels almost muscular to the touch, similar to beech bark. On older trees, it develops shallow furrows but never becomes deeply ridged.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Flat, papery seed pods 2-4 inches long that hang in clusters and rattle when dry. The pods split open to release 4-6 hard, brown seeds.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a broad, rounded crown with gracefully spreading branches. The trunk often divides low, creating a vase-like silhouette that's wider at the top than the bottom.

habitat: In New England, Kentucky yellowwood is found almost exclusively as a planted ornamental in parks, arboretums, and residential landscapes. It thrives in well-drained soils and full sun to partial shade. You're most likely to encounter it at botanical gardens or in suburban neighborhoods where it was planted for its ornamental value.

seasonality.spring: Spectacular drooping clusters of fragrant white flowers appear in late May to early June, covering the tree in cascades of pea-like blooms. New leaves emerge bright green and soft.
seasonality.summer: Full green foliage provides dense shade, while flat seed pods begin developing and hanging in clusters. The smooth gray bark is easily visible through the open canopy.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn bright golden-yellow before dropping, creating a stunning autumn display. The papery seed pods mature and begin rattling in the wind.
seasonality.winter: Smooth gray bark and graceful branching pattern are the main identifying features. Dried seed pods may persist on branches, rattling in winter winds.

funFact: Kentucky yellowwood trees are incredibly long-lived but bloom erratically - a mature tree might produce its spectacular flower show only every 2-3 years, making those blooming years especially magical for anyone lucky enough to witness the display.
confusionNotes: The drooping white flower clusters might be confused with black locust, but yellowwood flowers are much more densely packed and fragrant, while black locust has thorny branches and more open flower clusters. Remember: yellowwood is smooth and sweet-smelling, locust is thorny and less fragrant.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name, Kentucky yellowwood is quite rare even in its native range and is considered uncommon throughout its natural habitat. Most people in New England will only see this tree in cultivated settings, as it's prized by landscapers for its ornamental qualities but doesn't naturalize in our climate.
compareHints: Kentucky yellowwood is the only member of its genus found in North America, making it quite unique among our native trees. Within the legume family, it's most similar to black locust, but lacks the thorns and has much more impressive flower displays. Unlike other leguminous trees, yellowwood has perfectly smooth bark and never develops the rough, furrowed bark typical of locusts or honey locusts.
